title: How are people making genuinely good-looking games with Claude Opus 5.5?
author: Dismal-Reveal-6898
selftext:
I've been seeing people build some genuinely impressive games with Claude Opus 5.5, and I'm curious how you're actually pulling it off.

I'm working on my own games with AI, mainly in Unity, and while I can get the mechanics and basic gameplay working, getting everything to look and feel like a *real, polished game* is a completely different story.

Some of the AI-assisted projects I've seen have great lighting, detailed environments, smooth animations, realistic materials, and an actual atmosphere. Meanwhile, mine still tend to have that obvious indie/prototype look.

So I'm wondering, what's your actual workflow?

Are you letting Opus handle most of the development? Do you use Blender, asset packs, custom shaders, or other AI tools alongside it? And how much of the visual quality comes from prompting versus manually tweaking things?

I'm especially interested in horror games, where lighting, sound design, animations, and atmosphere make such a huge difference.

I'd love to hear from people who've managed to make something genuinely impressive. What made the biggest difference for you? Any prompts, workflows, tools, or tricks you'd recommend?

Basically, how do you go from "AI made a playable game" to "this actually looks and feels like something people would want to play"?

comments.author: Zimgar
comments.body:
Typically what I've seen is that those games that have 'slop' art, is because they don't know how art works in games.  That is they ask AI to generate something and then put that art in.  Which is like shoving concept art into a game, it doesn't look great, doesn't have the right feel.

Let's use 2D as an example, but 3D is typically the same, just different.

\- You start with a concept art of what you are looking to achieve.  
\- You then break down this concept art into the many different pieces that compose it.  
\- This is often several different 'layers' of images, that are then exported out separately and composed inside of the game engine.  
\- Your final game object is composed of many many game objects, images, glow effects, particle effects, materials.

Which you try to separate the gameplay aspect from the visual as much as possible... but I also tend to think the best games are those that 'mix' it a little as well.

So to have good AI art, my recommendation is first develop a concept of what you are going with.  Identify the art style you want, collect reference art for that art style.  Try to right down the features of that art you like and want.

Then do concept art for specific pieces, breakdown those pieces, then have it generate the art for those individual pieces.  The outcome will be a greater result.

comments.author: ThePubRelic

First step: Create a GDD  
Second step: Create a style bible  
Third step: Establish one example following style bible that visual meets your tastes and goals  
Fourth step: Iterate on each generated object, preferably adding controls to interact with the object to guide the LLM  
Fifth step: create dedicated pipelines that the LLM has proven it can follow without oversight

I think a lot of the very polished looking ones do one of these things:

1. use premade assets, the AI organizes them
2. Use screenshot mockups so the AI knows the gist of how it should look
3. Use other AI's likeTripo to make 3D assets

comments.author: bubuplush
comments.body:
Start with something simple and don't try to remake Skyrim, Star Citizen or The Witcher visuals. Do something like a Playstation X demake, a game in the style of an old GameBoy game, a 2D platformer or turn-based pixel RPG. Or, if you want something like Skyrim, try a Morrowind-like style instead. With AI coding being able to do so much for you, the only real thing you need to learn is how to make your own pretty assets, how to come up with a helpful UI design and how to balance player agency, engagement, reward and challenge

Right now it kinda sucks with humanoid 3D models imo, or at least it's rather complicated to tell opus to make, rig and animate a human player model. You can also use visual references. I literally just drew a house layout on paint with squares and rectangles, wrote the name of the furniture on top, provided 3D references of the furniture and claude made a really good looking house. Without that guidance it looked like shit

comments.author: Worried_Number5115
comments.body:
It takes continuous iteration. I’m 3 months into building my dream app and am going through visual upgrades. 

It is vastly based on your games design (I.e 2D top down, voxel art, 3D art, hyper realistic). Based on your existing visually design, you’ll want to work through adding in animations I. The form of ambient life, lighting, sound, shadows, idle movement, walk cycles, banners, nearly every visual component. 

I find it best to ask my LLM to scope a document based on what I want and my vision. It will highlight the decisions for me to make and I’ll ask for a rough draft of what this would look like if implements. Effectively I review and scope everything before putting it into the app. 

Takes a ton of time & iteration but way less than it would to hand code

comments.author: bestof-games
comments.body:
Ai answer from my game dev agent:

Solo dev here. Claude writes nearly all the code for my mobile games (Godot, not Unity, and no horror so far; one game is live on the App Store). I think the workflow carries over. What made my games look better wasn't better prompts. It was four things:

\*\*1. Let Claude see the game.\*\* This made the biggest difference. Out of the box Claude is blind: it writes a shader, says "this should look great", and has no idea that it doesn't. So I had it build a capture script. It loads the real game at the real device resolution, renders a few fixed camera shots and saves them as PNGs. Then the loop is: capture → Claude looks at the images next to reference images → lists the biggest gaps → fixes the top 2 → captures again. In Unity that's an editor script or a play-mode test that saves screenshots from fixed camera positions with post-processing on.

\*\*2. One look recipe for every asset, instead of tweaking them one by one.\*\* Assets that don't match are the main thing that makes a game look like a prototype. In my current game every 3D model goes through the same pipeline:  
\- Meshy text-to-3D, with the same style suffix on every prompt  
\- a headless Blender script that cuts off the base plate, fixes the origin, shrinks textures and decimates  
\- one shared toon shader in the engine. It blurs and posterizes the AI textures into one palette and gives everything the same light bands and rim light.

That shader is why 26 AI-generated models look like one set (about 880 Meshy credits for the whole set). The recipe is written down in the repo, so every new session follows it.

\*\*3. I'm the art director, Claude does the work.\*\* "Make it look polished" gets you something generic. What works for me is giving it a reference, then playing on the device and giving specific feedback: "outline too strong", "models hard to see", "world feels empty". Claude turns that into shader settings and light values. When there are several options, it renders a contact sheet (all candidates in one image) and I pick. Max 2 rounds per item. If it's still wrong after that, I bring a reference instead of trying a third time. I barely tweak anything by hand, but I look at things a lot.

\*\*4. Readability before looks, and test on the target device.\*\* My first 3D version looked worse than the flat 2D greybox: too busy, and you couldn't make out the models. A calm ground, bigger models and a thinner outline came before any extra effects. Things that look fine in the editor often fall apart on the real screen.

\*\*Animation:\*\* humanoid characters got an auto-rig plus clips (walk, idle, attack, death). Four-legged animals came out twisted on the biped rig, so they move in code instead (hop, squash and stretch, lunge). Small motion like sway, squash and idle breathing makes things feel alive for very little work.

\*\*For horror\*\* (I haven't tested this myself, but it's where I'd put the effort):  
\- Lighting is mostly about what you leave dark. Few light sources, a flashlight with a cookie, fog (real volumetric or faked) so the darkness has depth, and silhouettes you can still read.  
\- Pick a post stack and color grade early and write it into your look doc: grain, vignette, exposure, LUT. Use the same values everywhere.  
\- Sound is half the atmosphere, and Claude is good at building it as a system: ambient layers, 3D-positioned one-shot sounds, reverb zones, a "tension" value that fades layers in and out, and silence before a scare.  
\- In first person, camera motion (head bob, sway, breathing, footsteps in sync with steps) does more than character animation.

\*\*Workflow:\*\* Claude plans and writes almost all the code. I split the work into small rounds with clear "done when" criteria, play every build on my phone and make the calls. Keep a short CLAUDE.md in the repo with the look rules and past decisions, so new sessions don't slide back to the defaults.

TL;DR: screenshots in the loop, one look recipe for everything, and you make the taste calls.

comments.author: evangelism2
comments.body:
I went from zero knowledge of Blender to creating my first 3D model using it. It took me like 2.5 days, off and on, while working on other projects but I think it turned out really good for a mod for Valheim. That I made, the code took about an hour.

How did I do it? I applied the same troubleshooting and learning skills that I use daily in my job as a software developer to tackle this one step at a time. That's really how people do anything with AI.

AI rewards people who can take a big problem and break it down into smaller ones and people who have decent project management skills, organizational skills, note-taking skills, and research skills. You can use AI to help you develop those skills and expand upon them.

Nobody is going to give you their entire game dev workflow in a Reddit comment. They will give you some tips but ultimately it's up to you to take these tips and figure out which ones work for you, which ones don't, and to also just research game development as a whole.

You probably, if you're serious about this, are going to want to read a few books on the actual game development lifecycle or the software development lifecycle (so that you can learn how to apply those principles to your work with AI). AI is not magic. You can't just tell it, "Make me GTA 7, no bugs, thanks, please." You still have to direct it, maintain it, and manage it. It just allows you, as a single person, to do the work of 5 to 10 individuals as they would have done it 3 years ago.

comments.author: trentrez
comments.body:
Building a painterly open-world game this way (Claude Code, Opus for the visual work), so this is from doing it, not theorising.

The prototype look isn't a prompting problem, it's a review-loop problem. The model can't judge its own visuals — the thing it "saw" and the thing you see are different. What made the biggest difference:

1. **Art direction doc before anything**. One page: palette, light rig, post stack, mood, reference images, hard rules (fonts, camera, palette). Opus follows written constraints reliably and forgets spoken ones. Every visual session starts from that doc. Also: pick the direction by comparing 2–3 real options side by side, judge on screenshots, then lock it. Never re-litigate in chat.
2. **Iterate on screenshots**, not descriptions. Every visual change I review ships with a one-click URL with time of day, weather, and camera baked in, so I eyeball the exact same frame the model judged. Change → shot → human verdict → change. Most of "polish" is just many short loops with the human as the eye.
3. **The model proposes, you veto.** For look problems I do cheap R&D in chat first — diagnosis plus 2–3 options — then build one. Building a whole direction and then rejecting it is the expensive mistake.
4. **Rendering beats assets.** Atmosphere is mostly a small post stack (tone mapping, vignette, AO, fog, grain) plus a good light rig — not high-poly models. I use bought asset packs but run them through a converter into the game's own rig and style so everything reads as one set. Consistency beats fidelity.
5. **Restraint**. The prototype look is usually ten half-finished features. Do one thing until it's crisp, then add.

**For horror specifically:** the loop above is visual-only, and horror lives in sound and pacing. Record clips, judge with headphones, and treat audio passes like screenshot passes — that's the one everyone skips.

**Also worth it:** cheap model for mechanics (deepseek flash / haiku) and boilerplate, Opus only for look work and hard problems. None of this is one big prompt — it's many small sessions, and your eyes / ears / playtesting is the iterator
